title: Ivacaftor, a CFTR potentiator, synergizes with osimertinib against acquired resistance to osimertinib in NSCLC by regulating CFTR-PTEN-AKT axis
author: Yue-kang Li; Fu-jing Ge; Xiang-ning Liu; Chen-ming Zeng; Mei-jia Qian; Yong-hao Li; Ming-ming Zheng; Jing-jing Qu; Liang-jie Fang; Jin-jian Lu; Bo Yang; Qiao-jun He; Jian-ya Zhou; Hong Zhu
text:
Abstract
Osimertinib, a third-generation epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor (EGFR-TKI), has demonstrated significant clinical benefits in the treatment of EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). However, inevitable acquired resistance to osimertinib limits its clinical utility, and there is a lack of effective countermeasures. Here, we established osimertinib-resistant cell lines and performed drug library screening. This screening identified ivacaftor, a cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) potentiator, as a synergistic enhancer of osimertinib-induced anti-tumor activity both in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, ivacaftor facilitated the colocalization of CFTR and PTEN on the plasma membrane to promote the function of PTEN, subsequently inhibiting the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway and suppressing tumor growth. In summary, our study suggests that activating CFTR enhances osimertinib-induced anti-tumor activity by regulating the PTEN-AKT axis. Furthermore, ivacaftor and osimertinib constitute a potential combination strategy for treating osimertinib-resistant EGFR-mutated NSCLC patients.
Keywords: NSCLC, osimertinib, acquired resistance, ivacaftor, CFTR
Introduction
Lung cancer is one of the most prevalent malignancies and the primary cause of cancer-related death worldwide [1], and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for ~85% of all lung cancer cases [2]. The emergence of targeted therapy has considerably improved the prognosis of NSCLC patients with positive driver gene mutations, especially those with EGFR mutations, which are observed in almost 50% of Asian NSCLC patients [3]. Osimertinib, a third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (EGFR-TKI), was developed to overcome the acquired resistance associated with previous generations of EGFR-TKIs. It has been approved as the first-line treatment for EGFR-mutant NSCLC patients and exhibits remarkable clinical efficacy [4–6].
However, acquired resistance to osimertinib inevitably develops during its application and remains an unresolved challenge. The main mechanisms of acquired resistance to osimertinib can be divided into two forms: EGFR-dependent and EGFR-independent [7]. Among them, EGFR-dependent mechanisms (secondary mutations in EGFR, such as C797X, L792X, and G796X) account for only 10%–26% of cases, whereas EGFR-independent mechanisms (e.g., bypass pathways activation, phenotypic transformation) constitute the majority [8, 9]. The majority of EGFR-independent mechanisms of acquired resistance to osimertinib are attributed to MET amplification, HER2 amplification, PI3K pathway activation, RET gene fusions, AXL overexpression, and other factors. These mechanisms are associated with excessive downstream activation of the PI3K/AKT pathway [7, 9]. In general, it is crucial to discover combination treatments that target not only EGFR but also the PI3K/AKT pathway to overcome acquired resistance to osimertinb.
The phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/v-akt murine thymoma viral oncogene homolog (AKT) signaling pathway is abnormally activated in various cancers and plays a critical role in the occurrence and progression of diverse tumors [10]. However, the majority of AKT inhibitors have remained in the clinical trial stage, with only capivasertib being approved by the FDA this year exclusively for combination therapy with fulvestrant in the treatment of breast cancer [11, 12]. The termination of the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway is achieved mainly by PTEN, which dephosphorylates phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-trisphosphate (PIP3) to phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) [13]. Nevertheless, PTEN targeting remains an unresolved challenge because of its characteristics as a tumor suppressor and the complexity of its regulation and translational modifications [14, 15]. Overall, there is still a lack of effective strategies for targeting the PTEN/AKT signaling axis in NSCLC. We hypothesize that targeting the PTEN-AKT axis could effectively suppress the bypass activation of the PI3K/AKT pathway in EGFR-mutated NSCLC, thereby synergistically enhancing the anti-tumor activity of osimertinib. In this study, we performed drug library screening to identify a novel combination treatment for acquired resistance to osimertinib and conducted mechanistic investigations to elucidate the PTEN-AKT axis as a potential target for osimertinib-resistant (OR) NSCLC patients.
Materials and methods
Reagents and antibodies
Ivacaftor, osimertinib, lumacaftor, and SF1670 were purchased from MedChem Express (Princeton, NJ, USA). The primary antibodies used for Western blot analysis were as follows: p-AKT (Thr 308) (#13038), AKT (#4691), CFTR (#78335) and p-EGFR (Tyr 1068) (#3777) antibodies were purchased from Cell Signaling Technology (Danvers, MA, USA); and GAPDH (#db106) and Flag (#db7002) antibodies were purchased from Diagbio Bioscience (Hangzhou, China). For immunofluorescence, primary antibodies against CFTR (#sc-376683) and PTEN (#A11193) were purchased from Santa Cruz Biotechnology (Santa Cruz, CA, USA) and ABclonal Technology (Wuhan, China), respectively; DAPI (#EF704) was purchased from Dojindo Molecular Technologies (Tokyo, Japan); and Alexa Fluor 488 donkey anti-mouse (#A-21202) and Alexa Fluor 568 donkey anti-rabbit (#A-10042) secondary antibodies were purchased from Thermo Fisher Scientific (Waltham, MA, USA). For immunohistochemistry, the primary antibody against Ki-67 (#sc-23900) was purchased from Santa Cruz Biotechnology (Santa Cruz, CA, USA), and the HRP-conjugated secondary antibody (PV-6001) and 3,3′-diaminobenzidine tetrahydrochloride chromogen (DAB) kit (#ZLI-9018) were purchased from ZSGB-BIO Company (Beijing, China).
Cell culture
The human NSCLC cell line PC-9 and the human embryonic kidney cell line HEK293FT were obtained from the Shanghai Institute of Biochemistry and Cell Biology (Shanghai, China). The human NSCLC cell lines NCI-H1975 and HCC827 were obtained from Dr. Jin-jian Lu at the University of Macau (Macau, China). NCI-H1975-OR, HCC827-OR, and PC-9-OR cells were established from their parental cells via dosage-escalation of osimertinib from 10 nM to 1 μM over ~6 months (Fig. 1a). All the NSCLC cell lines were cultured in RPMI-1640 medium (Gibco, Grand Island, NY, USA) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (Gibco), whereas the HEK293FT cells were cultured in DMEM medium (Gibco) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum. All the cells were cultured at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere of 5% CO2, and the presence of mycoplasma was routinely monitored every 6 months. All the cell lines were authenticated via short tandem repeat (STR) profiling.
Plasmids and transduction
Human CFTR was tagged with 3×Flag at the C-terminus and inserted into pcDNA3.1, which was purchased from GeneCopoeia (Guangzhou, China). The lentiviral vector pCDH-EF1-Puro plasmid was obtained from Addgene (Watertown, MA, USA).
To stably overexpress the target protein in cells, the lentiviral cloning vector pCDH-EF1-Puro encoding the target protein was cotransfected with the packaging vector pCMV-dR8.91 and the envelope vector pMD2-VSVG into HEK293FT cells to produce lentivirus stocks. For transduction, target cells at a confluency of 20% were exposed to 1–2 mL of virus-containing polybrene (8 μg/mL) for 18–24 h. The culture medium was subsequently replaced with fresh medium.
Cell viability assay
NCI-H1975-OR, HCC827-OR, PC-9-OR, and their parental cells were plated in 96-well plates at 2000 cells/well and treated with serial concentrations of agents the next day. Cell viability was measured via a sulforhodamin B (SRB) staining assay or a Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) from Beyotime Biotechnology (Shanghai, China) after treatment for 48 or 72 h. The SRB staining assay was performed as described previously [16]. To evaluate the synergistic effect, the combination index (CI) value was calculated via CalcuSyn software [17, 18], or the coefficient of drug interaction (CDI) value was calculated via the following formula: OD values of each group, AB represents the survival rate of the combination treatment group compared with the control group, and A or B represents the survival rate of each monotherapy group compared with the control group.
Drug library construction and screening
The small molecule drug library was purchased from Topscience (Shanghai, China) and contained 100 FDA-approved drugs (Table S1). Two rounds of drug screening were performed. In the first round, NCI-H1975-OR cells were plated in 96-well plates at 1500 cells/well and treated with 0.5 μM osimertinib plus each library drug at 50 μM for 48 h. Library drugs exhibiting a combined inhibition of over 60% with osimertinib were selected for the subsequent round of screening. In the second round, the NCI-H1975-OR cells were plated in 96-well plates at 1500 cells/well and treated with 0.5 μM osimertinib, 20 μM candidate library drugs, or both for 48 h. Cell viability was assessed via an SRB staining assay, and the CDI values for each combination group were calculated as described previously.
Colony formation assay
The lentivirus-infected NCI-H1975-OR, HCC827-OR, and PC-9-OR cells and their parental cells were plated in 12-well plates at 2000 cells/well and treated with agents the next day. After 72 h, the medium supplemented with drugs was replaced with fresh medium, and the cells were cultured for 14 days. The cells were stained with SRB, photographed, and then dissolved in 1% Tris-base for quantification analysis.
EdU incorporation assay
The EdU incorporation assay was performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions for the BeyoClickTM EdU-488 Imaging Kit (Beyotime Biotechnology, Shanghai, China). The cells were exposed to 10 μM EdU for 2 h before being fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde at room temperature for 15 min. The cells were then permeabilized with 0.3% Triton-X for 15 min, followed by incubation with click reaction solution (a mixture of click reaction buffer, CuSO4, azide 488, and click additive solution) at room temperature in the dark for 30 min. Afterward, the cell nuclei were stained with Hoechst 33342, and fluorescence was detected.
Cell apoptosis analysis
The cells were collected after drug exposure and washed with PBS. The cells were subsequently stained with Annexin V-FITC and propidium iodide (PI) via an Annexin V-FITC Apoptosis Detection Kit (Beyotime Biotechnology, Shanghai, China) at room temperature in the dark for 15 min. Subsequently, cell apoptosis was analyzed using a CytoFLEX flow cytometer (Beckman Coulter, Brea, CA, USA).
Western blot analysis
The cell lysates were resolved by 10% SDS-PAGE and transferred to polyvinylidene fluoride membranes (Millipore Corporation, Billerica, MA, USA). The target membrane was subsequently incubated with the indicated primary antibodies and HRP-labeled secondary antibodies. The chemiluminescence signal was detected using an AI600 system (GE Healthcare Inc., Boston, MA, USA) following incubation-enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL).
Immunofluorescence
NCI-H1975-OR, NCI-H1975-S, HCC827-OR, and HCC827-S cells were plated in fluorescent chamber slides and exposed to the indicated drugs the next day for 24 h. Immunofluorescence was performed as described previously [19]. To evaluate the colocalization of CFTR and PTEN, photographs were analyzed, and Pearson’s correlation coefficient (PCC) values were calculated via ImageJ software.
Animal xenograft model
All animal experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of Zhejiang University (Hangzhou, China). Female 4–6 weeks old BALB/c-Nude mice were obtained from Zhejiang Chinese Medical University (Hangzhou, China). The mice were injected subcutaneously with 5.0 × 106 HCC827-OR or HCC827-S cells. When the tumors reached an average volume of 75.0 mm3, the mice were randomized into the indicated groups (n = 5/group) to receive vehicle (0.5% CMC-Na), osimertinib (5 mg/kg or 0.5 mg/kg), ivacaftor (50 mg/kg) or combination treatment every day. Tumor volume and body weight were measured every two days. The tumor volume and relative tumor volume (RTV) were calculated via the following formulas:
Immunohistochemistry
Immunohistochemistry was performed as described previously [19]. To quantify the Ki-67 positive cells, images of the immunohistochemistry results were analyzed via Image Pro Plus software.
RNA sequencing and analysis
Total RNA was extracted from the HCC827-OR cell-derived xenograft (CDX) tumor tissue via TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA). The library was constructed following Illumina® Stranded mRNA Prep, Ligation (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA), and sequencing was performed on the NovaSeq X Plus platform using the NovaSeq Reagent Kit (Illumina) at Shanghai Majorbio Bio-pharm Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). The raw paired-end reads were trimmed and quality controlled using “fastp” software. The clean reads were individually aligned to the reference genome using “HISAT2” software, and “StringTie” software was used to assemble the mapped reads of each sample. The expression level of each transcript was calculated according to the transcripts per million reads (TPM) method to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between different samples. DEGs with a fold change >2 or <0.5 with a P value < 0.05 were considered significantly DEGs. Subsequently, functional enrichment analysis of the significantly DEGs was conducted via the “clusterProfiler” package (version 4.6.0) against the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) and Gene Ontology (GO) databases, and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was also performed via the ‘clusterProfiler’ package (version 4.6.0). All the results were displayed with the ‘ggplot2’ package (version 3.4.2) in R software.
Statistical analysis
Statistical analysis was performed, and the data were plotted via GraphPad 8 software. When comparing data between two groups, statistical significance was calculated using an unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-test. When comparing data from three or more groups, one-way ANOVA and Tukey’s multiple comparisons test were used to calculate the statistical significance. The log-rank test was used to compare the survival data via Kaplan–Meier analysis. The data are presented as the means ± SDs, and the results were considered statistically significant when P < 0.05 (*, P < 0.05; **, P < 0.01; ***, P < 0.001).
Results
Establishment of the HCC827-OR, NCI-H1975-OR and PC9-OR cell lines
To establish OR NSCLC cell lines, three different osimertinib-sensitive (OS) cell lines with two mutation backgrounds, namely, HCC827 (EGFR exon 19 deletion), PC-9 (EGFR exon 19 deletion) and NCI-H1975 (EGFR exon 20 T790M and exon 21 L858R mutation), were selected. The OS cell lines were exposed to osimertinib at concentrations ranging from 10 nM to 1 μM for nearly 6 months to induce osimertinib resistance (Fig. 1a). All the cell lines were treated with serial concentrations of osimertinib for 72 h, and the surviving fraction of the cells following treatment was measured via an SRB staining assay. Dose-survival curves revealed that the HCC827-OR, NCI-H1975-OR, and PC-9-OR cell lines exhibited significantly greater cell viability than did their parental cell lines after the same treatment (Fig. 1b). In addition, we calculated the half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) of osimertinib for each cell line. The IC50 values of osimertinib for HCC827-OR and HCC827-S cells were 2425 nM and 3.006 nM, respectively; those for NCI-H1975-OR and NCI-H1975-S cells were 971.8 nM and 3.687 nM, respectively; and those for PC-9-OR and PC-9-S cells were 559.5 nM and 4.487 nM, respectively (Fig. 1c). The resistance factors (RFs) of the HCC827-OR, NCI-H1975-OR and PC-9-OR cell lines all exceeded 100, indicating the successful establishment of these three OR cell lines.
The mutation and proliferation statuses of the OR cell lines were subsequently examined. The meaningful EGFR mutations mainly occur in exons 18–21, which encode the intracellular tyrosine kinase domain of EGFR. Therefore, Sanger sequencing of EGFR exons 18–21 was performed on three OR cell lines and their respective parental OS cell lines, revealing no secondary EGFR mutations in the OR cell lines compared with their parental cell lines (Fig. 1d). This result indicated that the acquired resistance to osimertinib in our three self-established OR cell lines was mediated by EGFR-independent mechanisms, such as bypass pathway activation. In addition, all the cell lines were seeded at the same density, and their growth rates were evaluated via an SRB staining assay. The results indicated that HCC827-OR and NCI-H1975-OR cells exhibited significantly accelerated growth compared with their parental cells, while the growth rate of PC-9-OR cells was similar to that of PC-9-S cells (Fig. S1a).
Drug-library screening identifies ivacaftor as a potential enhancer of osimertinib-induced anti-tumor activity
To identify potential synergistic strategies to overcome osimertinib resistance, we performed a drug screening using a self-established drug library containing 100 FDA-approved drugs (Table S1). Two rounds of screening were performed, as shown in the flowchart in Fig. 2a, and crizotinib was selected as a positive control, which exhibited clinical efficacy in combination with osimertinib in EGFR TKI-resistant NSCLC patients [20–22]. In the first round, NCI-H1975-OR cells were exposed to osimertinib (0.5 μM) plus a high concentration (50 μM) of each drug from the library for 48 h, and fifteen candidate drugs with a combined inhibition rate of over 60% were screened out (Fig. 2b). In the second round, NCI-H1975-OR cells were exposed to osimertinib (0.5 μM), each candidate drug screened out in the first round (20 μM), or both for 48 h, and cell viability was determined using an SRB staining assay. The CDI values of each drug combined with osimertinib were calculated, and a lower CDI value indicates stronger drug synergism. Among the top 15 hit drugs, the positive control crizotinib exhibited the minimal CDI value of 0.31, followed by indacaterol and ivacaftor, with CDI values of ~0.5 (0.47 and 0.51, Fig. 2c), and the top 15 hit drugs with their targets were listed in Fig. 2d. However, Li et al. [23] reported that indacaterol can enhance osimertinib-induced cell growth inhibition in EGFR-TKI-resistant NSCLC cells, and this enhancement was achieved through a potential mechanism in which indacaterol binds within the ATP-binding cavity of EGFR L858R/T790M, thereby inhibiting the enzymatic activity of the mutant kinase. Therefore, the cystic fibrosis (CF) transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) potentiator ivacaftor (Fig. 2e) was identified as a potent drug that synergistically enhanced osimertinib-induced cell growth inhibition in OR NSCLC cell lines through our drug library screening.
The combination of ivacaftor and osimertinib results in synergistic anti-tumor activity in vitro
To evaluate the combined effect of ivacaftor and osimertinib in OR NSCLC cell lines, HCC827-OR, NCI-H1975-OR, and PC-9-OR cells were treated with serial concentrations of ivacaftor, osimertinib, or both for 72 h, and the cell survival fraction of each treatment group was detected using an SRB staining assay. The dose-survival curves of each treatment group are shown in Fig. 3a, which indicates that compared with monotherapy, combination therapy of ivacaftor and osimertinib significantly reduced the survival fraction of OR NSCLC cells. Furthermore, to obtain an accurate evaluation of the synergistic anti-tumor effect, the CI values were calculated at each concentration ratio of ivacaftor to osimertinib via CalcuSyn software [17]. Because a CI value less than 1.0 indicates synergistic effects, most CI values in all three cell lines, HCC827-OR, NCI-H1975-OR, and PC-9-OR, were less than 1.0 (Fig. 3b). Furthermore, both the CCK-8 assay and the EdU incorporation assay confirmed that the combination of ivacaftor and osimertinib significantly inhibited the proliferation of HCC827-OR, NCI-H1975-OR and PC-9-OR cells (Fig. 3c, d). In addition, the combination of ivacaftor and osimertinib significantly increased the percentage of apoptotic HCC827-OR, NCI-H1975-OR, and PC-9-OR cells (Fig. 3g). These findings demonstrated the synergistic anti-tumor activity of ivacaftor and osimertinib in OR NSCLC cells.
In addition, we conducted a colony formation assay to investigate the long-term synergistic effect of ivacaftor and osimertinib. Representative photographs at the endpoint are depicted in Fig. 3e, indicating that the combination therapy resulted in substantially greater inhibition than either monotherapy. Further calculations of the colony formation rates confirmed that the combination of ivacaftor and osimertinib had a significantly stronger long-term anti-tumor effect than either monotherapy in OR NSCLC cells (Fig. 3f). This long-term synergistic effect was also observed in OS NSCLC cells (Fig. S2a). In summary, ivacaftor synergistically enhanced osimertinib-induced anti-tumor activity in both OR and OS NSCLC cells in vitro.
Ivacaftor synergistically enhances osimertinib-induced anti-tumor activity in vivo
To evaluate the synergistic anti-tumor efficacy of ivacaftor and osimertinib in vivo, an HCC827-OR CDX nude mouse model was established. The mice were randomly divided into four groups (n = 5/group) and treated daily with 50 mg/kg ivacaftor, 5 mg/kg osimertinib, or a combination of both drugs or solvent as a control (Fig. 4a). As shown in Fig. 4b–e, all the therapies remarkably inhibited tumor growth, while the combination of ivacaftor and osimertinib resulted in significantly greater tumor inhibition than either monotherapy alone. Furthermore, no significant body weight loss was observed in the mice treated with ivacaftor, osimertinib or their combination (Fig. 4f), suggesting the safety profile of this combination treatment. An H&E staining assay and an immunohistochemistry analysis also revealed a greater presence of necrotic tumor foci and a significant decrease in Ki-67 expression in the combination group than in the other individual treatment groups (Fig. 4g–h). The in vivo efficacy and safety of this combined therapy were also observed in an HCC827-S CDX nude mouse model (Fig. S3a–g).
In summary, ivacaftor significantly enhanced osimertinib-induced anti-tumor activity in both OR and OS EGFR-mutated NSCLC in vivo.
To further investigate the potential molecular mechanism of the synergistic enhancement of osimertinib-induced anti-tumor activity by ivacaftor, we compared the transcriptomes of HCC827-OR CDX tumors treated with combination therapy or osimertinib monotherapy, and performed KEGG enrichment analysis on the significantly DEGs, which indicated that these genes were significantly enriched in the PI3K-AKT signaling pathway (Fig. 4i). Moreover, the GSEA results revealed significant downregulation of the PI3K-AKT signaling pathway and EGFR-TKI resistance related pathways in the combination group compared with those in the osimertinib group (Fig. 4j). The normalized enrichment scores (NES) of the PI3K-AKT signaling pathway and EGFR-TKI resistance related pathways were −1.20 and −1.49, respectively. These results suggest that ivacaftor may synergistically counteract osimertinib resistance by inhibiting the PI3K-AKT signaling pathway.
Ivacaftor facilitates the plasma membrane localization of PTEN and synergizes with osimertinib to dephosphorylate the PI3K-AKT signaling pathway
CFTR is an anion channel belonging to the adenosine triphosphate binding cassette (ABC) transporter superfamily [24]. The main functions of CFTR are transporting chloride ions from the interior of epithelial cells to the exterior and regulating other ion channels, which play crucial roles in maintaining the functionality of epithelial cells and maintaining tissue homeostasis in vital organs such as the lungs [25]. Dysfunctions of CFTR caused by gene mutations are the fundamental pathogenesis of CF [26].
In addition, Riquelme et al. [27] reported that CFTR directly interacts with the tumor suppressor PTEN and helps position PTEN at the membrane to promote its function in host immunity against infection. Our transcriptome analysis results suggested significant downregulation of the PI3K-AKT signaling pathway in the combination group compared with the osimertinib group (Fig. 4i–j), and we hypothesized that the CFTR potentiator ivacaftor may regulate the CFTR-PTEN-AKT axis in NSCLC cells to synergize with osimertinib.
We first assessed the baseline AKT phosphorylation levels in HCC827-OR, NCI-H1975-OR, and corresponding parental cell lines via Western blot analysis (Fig. 5a). The level of AKT phosphorylation was markedly greater in OR cells than in parental cells, indicating that the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway was excessively activated in our OR cell lines. We observed that AKT phosphorylation was completely inhibited by osimertinib in HCC827-S and NCI-H1975-S cells but was partially reduced in OR cells (Fig. 5b). Besides, EGFR phosphorylation in OR cells was completely inhibited under the same osimertinib treatment conditions (Fig. S4a). These results indicated that overactivation of the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, which is one of the major bypass pathways involved in EGFR-independent resistance to osimertinib, was responsible for the acquired resistance of our self-established OR cell lines, rather than the secondary mutation of EGFR. Moreover, the combination of ivacaftor and osimertinib synergistically inhibited AKT phosphorylation more effectively than each individual drug did in OR cells (Fig. 5c). Additionally, the ivacaftor-mediated inhibition of the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway could be reversed by the PTEN inhibitor SF1670 in HCC827-OR and NCI-H1975-OR cells (Fig. 5d). Both the cell proliferation and colony formation abilities of these OR cells were significantly rescued by SF1670 compared with the combination therapy of ivacaftor and osimertinib (Fig. 5e–g). These results suggested that ivacaftor synergistically inhibited the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway and enhanced osimertinib-induced anti-tumor activity through PTEN.
To further elucidate the mechanism by which ivacaftor synergistically inhibits overactivation of the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway in combination with osimertinib, an immunofluorescence assay was conducted to examine the cellular localization of CFTR (green) and PTEN (red) with or without ivacaftor. The overlapping signal (yellow) revealed intense colocalization between CFTR and PTEN in both NCI-H1975-OR and NCI-H1975-S cells (Fig. 5h). The PCC value is used to quantify the degree of colocalization, and a PCC value > 0.5 indicates colocalization [28, 29]. In accordance with previous reports demonstrating a direct interaction between CFTR and PTEN, which is necessary to position PTEN at the membrane [27], CFTR and PTEN exhibited a high degree of colocalization in NCI-H1975-S (PCC = 0.63 ± 0.17) and NCI-H1975-OR (PCC = 0.53 ± 0.16) cells (Fig. 5i). Furthermore, colocalization significantly increased after exposure to ivacaftor in both NCI-H1975-S (PCC = 0.73 ± 0.13 versus 0.63 ± 0.17, P = 0.015) and NCI-H1975-OR cells (PCC = 0.67 ± 0.09 versus 0.53 ± 0.16, P < 0.001). Since the membrane localization of PTEN is required for its tumor suppressor function [30, 31], we detected the subcellular localization of PTEN. A substantial fraction of PTEN colocalized with CFTR at the plasma membrane in the ivacaftor treatment groups, whereas a major proportion of PTEN was localized in the nucleus in the control groups (Fig. 5j). Similar results were also observed in HCC827-S and HCC827-OR cells (Fig. S5a–b). Moreover, the protein level of PTEN was unaffected by drug treatment in OR cells, suggesting that ivacaftor altered only the subcellular localization of PTEN without affecting its expression level (Fig. S6a).
Overall, these findings suggested that ivacaftor markedly enhanced the colocalization of CFTR and PTEN, facilitating the plasma membrane localization of PTEN, thereby synergistically inhibiting AKT phosphorylation with osimertinib, which promoted osimertinib-induced anti-tumor activity in OR cell lines.
CFTR enhances the anti-tumor activity of osimertinib in OR NSCLC cells
To confirm that ivacaftor synergizes with osimertinib through the CFTR-PTEN-AKT axis rather than through off-target effects, we further investigated the critical role of CFTR in OR NSCLC. First, we established vector or CFTR overexpressing stable HCC827-OR and NCI-H1975-OR cell lines. The efficacy of CFTR overexpression was confirmed, and the level of AKT phosphorylation was substantially decreased in CFTR overexpressing cells, whereas the protein level of PTEN remained unaffected (Figs. 6a and S7a). Additionally, the overexpression of CFTR significantly inhibited the proliferation of HCC827-OR and NCI-H1975-OR cells (Fig. 6b). More potent anti-tumor efficacy was also observed in CFTR overexpressing stable HCC827-OR and NCI-H1975-OR cells under the same conditions of osimertinib exposure (Fig. 6c, d). To further verify the synergistic effect of ivacaftor and osimertinib in relation to CFTR, we selected lumacaftor [32], a CFTR corrector, to combine with osimertinib. Compared with osimertinib monotherapy, the combination of lumacaftor and osimertinib resulted in enhanced anti-tumor activity, as evidenced by CDI values < 1.0 at all the tested dose combinations (Fig. S8a, b), indicating that lumacaftor also synergistically enhanced the anti-tumor activity of osimertinib. At the patient level, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the correlation between CFTR mRNA levels and overall survival (OS) in NSCLC patients via data from the Kaplan-Meier plotter database (Fig. 6e). Our analysis revealed that the hazard ratio of CFTR was 0.7, confirming that its high expression was significantly correlated with an improved prognosis in NSCLC patients (P = 2.2×e − 07).
These findings indicate that CFTR possesses tumor-suppressive activity in NSCLC while synergistically enhancing the anti-tumor activity of osimertinib, which playes a critical role in combination therapy of ivacaftor and osimertinib.
Discussion
Osimertinib is currently a first-line treatment option for advanced EGFR-mutated NSCLC patients and exhibits remarkable survival benefits. However, the challenge of acquired resistance is common. The development of next-generation EGFR-TKIs has focused primarily on patients with EGFR-dependent resistance mechanisms, such as the C797S mutation, and these molecules are still in clinical trials or preclinical stages [33–35]. Although combination therapies targeting MET, HER2 or other genes have been used in OR patients with associated bypass activation, the population benefiting from these approaches is limited [36]. Here, we established 3 OR cell lines through a dosage-escalation method and performed FDA-approved drug library screening to identify therapeutic agents that synergize with osimertinib in OR NSCLC. Through this approach, the CFTR potentiator ivacaftor has been shown to synergistically enhance the anti-tumor efficacy of osimertinib by activating the CFTR-PTEN-AKT axis.
There is substantial evidence indicating the CFTR is a tumor suppressor in multiple cancers, such as gastrointestinal cancer, breast cancer, and others [37–39]. In NSCLC, promoter hypermethylation of the CFTR gene leads to reduced expression of CFTR in the tumor tissues of NSCLC patients [40]. Low CFTR expression is significantly associated with poor prognosis in NSCLC patients [41, 42]. These findings suggest a definite tumor-suppressive function of CFTR in NSCLC. Activating CFTR has also been shown to inhibit the proliferation of glioblastoma and lung adenocarcinoma cells [42, 43]. However, it remains unknown whether there is a correlation between CFTR and sensitivity to NSCLC treatments, such as EGFR-TKIs. Through our drug library screening, CFTR potentiator ivacaftor was shown to synergistically enhance the anti-tumor activity of osimertinib in OR NSCLC. Similarly, in a high-throughput screening to identify therapeutic agents that synergize with osimertinib to eliminate EGFR-mutant NSCLC, molecules that target CFTR ranked among the top [44]. We further confirmed that the overexpression of CFTR or lumacaftor, another CFTR corrector, can also effectively enhance the anti-tumor activity of osimertinib. These findings confirmed the crucial role of CFTR in suppressing EGFR-mutant NSCLC and demonstrated that activating CFTR serves as an effective strategy to tackle acquired resistance to osimertinib.
Moreover, we observed that baseline CFTR expression was lower in OR cells than in their parental cells, which may further promote excessive activation of the downstream PI3K/AKT pathway (Fig. 5a). Similarly, previous studies reported a corresponding increase in P-glycoprotein (P-gp, MDR1) protein levels and a significant decrease in CFTR protein levels in resistant colon adenocarcinoma cells [45, 46]. The MDR1 protein is also a member of the ABC transporter superfamily, similar to CFTR, which shares a homologous structure with CFTR, except for the absence of the R domain, and its efflux pump function mediates the occurrence and development of resistance to various chemotherapy drugs in multiple types of cancer [47–49]. In addition, a complementary pattern of expression was discovered between the MDR1 protein and CFTR, whereby the upregulation of the MDR1 protein led to the downregulation of CFTR [50]. Therefore, we hypothesize that exposure to osimertinib leads to the upregulation of MDR1 expression in NSCLC cells, resulting in the downregulation of CFTR expression, further affecting its regulation of the downstream PTEN-AKT axis and thereby promoting the occurrence and development of osimertinib resistance. Further experiments are planned to validate our aforementioned hypothesis.
The PI3K/AKT pathway is a crucial downstream pathway overactivated in multiple mechanisms of acquired resistance to osimertinib [7]. Excessive phosphorylation of AKT has also been observed in our self-established OR NSCLC cell lines, which cannot be completely suppressed by monotherapy of osimertinib, suggesting bypass overactivation of the PI3K/AKT pathway in our OR cell lines. Meanwhile, we confirmed that there were no secondary EGFR mutations in our OR cell lines through Sanger sequencing (Fig. 1d). Therefore, bypass pathway activation may be the main reason for the acquired resistance to osimertinib in our self-established OR cell lines. Besides, stronger bypass overactivation of the PI3K/AKT pathway was observed in HCC827-OR cells, which presented the highest resistance factor (RF = 807) (Fig. 5b), which may explain why the growth rate of the HCC827-OR cell line was greater than that of its parental cell line. Conversely, the growth rate of the PC-9-OR cell line with the lowest resistance factor (RF = 125) was similar to that of the PC-9-S cell line (Fig. S1a). As a result, we speculate that the changes in the growth rates of the OR cell lines compared with their parental cell lines may be correlated with the extent of proliferation-associated bypass pathway activation.
PTEN, a classical tumor suppressor, inhibits AKT activity by dephosphorylating PIP3 on the plasma membrane [13]. Therefore, the membrane localization of PTEN is essential for its active form [31]. Previous studies have indicated that CFTR interacts directly with PTEN and helps position it at the plasma membrane, promoting its anti-inflammatory function against Pseudomonas aeruginosa in monocytic cells [27, 51]. We further validated the colocalization of CFTR and PTEN in NSCLC cells and discovered that the CFTR potentiator ivacaftor promoted the colocalization of CFTR and PTEN. Additionally, the PTEN protein levels in our OR cells were not affected by ivacaftor, whereas Riquelme et al. [27] reported that CFTR corrector-potentiator therapy could increase the amount of PTEN in CF patients. Importantly, their results suggested that the ability of CFTR potentiators to increase the amount of PTEN may be associated with the type of CFTR mutation in targeted cells. The amount of PTEN was not affected by corrector-potentiator therapy in cells with some specific CFTR mutations. Moreover, in those cells where CFTR potentiators increased the amount of PTEN, the potentiators can restore the amount of PTEN to the level observed in wild-type CFTR cells [27]. Thus, it appeared reasonable that only the localization of PTEN was regulated by ivacaftor in our NSCLC cells with wild-type CFTR, while the amount of PTEN remained unaffected. As a result, ivacaftor enhances the plasma membrane localization of PTEN, thereby synergistically inhibiting overactivation of the PI3K/AKT pathway with osimertinib in OR cell lines. In addition, there is currently a lack of effective strategies targeting PTEN, while AKT inhibitors are either in clinical trials or preclinical stages. Our study also provides a novel strategy for targeting the PTEN-PI3K/AKT axis through the activation of CFTR with FDA-approved drugs.
Conclusions
In conclusion, our study identifies ivacaftor as a therapeutic agent that synergistically enhances the anti-tumor activity of osimertinib by regulating the CFTR-PTEN-AKT axis in EGFR-mutated NSCLC both in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, the activation of CFTR promotes the function of PTEN, thereby inhibiting the downstream PI3K/AKT pathway and suppressing tumor growth. Our study provides preclinical evidence for combining osimertinib and CFTR targeting as a potential strategy to overcome acquired resistance to osimertinib in EGFR-mutated NSCLC.
